newsitem.title: UK: West wants more action on E.European corruption.
newsitem.headline: West wants more action on E.European corruption.

text.p: Western bankers and officials warned the former communist countries of central and eastern Europe on Monday that they needed to act more vigorously to stamp out corruption and inefficiency.

At the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the United States told Russia it would continue haemorrhaging cash until it established a satisfactory financial regulatory system.

Germany said the EBRD, set up in 1991 to help the former Soviet bloc make the transition to market economies, should start letting the most advanced countries -- generally understood to mean the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary -- stand on their own feet.
But Slovakia said this would be premature.
A constant theme at the start of the two-day annual meeting was the need to stamp out fraud and corruption.
EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere listed legal uncertainties, taxation systems and corruption as major obstacles deterring foreign investors.
"There is corruption, crime and the arbitrary interference of some officials in private sector business activities," he said.
"Although these are far from being the rule, they remain a source of concern and have, in some cases, complicated or even compromised the bank's own operations."
There was praise for President Boris Yeltsin's renewed commitment to economic reform in Russia and the United States said his recent appointees were "a new economic dream team."

But the U.S. representative, assistant Treasury secretary David Lipton, said Russia would still scare off foreign investors and fail to prevent its own people sending their money abroad unless it established proper financial regulation.
"In the absence of that, and until that is secured...there will be some capital outflow," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"What we have is an interesting situation where Russians are saving and, like foreign investors, are not willing to put all of their money into Russian investments."
German finance ministry state secretary Juergen Stark said the EBRD should scale down its activities in the most successful countries in favour of the weaker ones.
"The Bank must begin to withdraw from operations in the advanced central European countries, for which an increasing volume of private finance is on hand," he said.
"This means that the regional emphasis of the Bank's operations will shift further eastwards."
But his Slovak counterpart, Tatiana Silhankova, objected.
"It certainly seems premature to consider suspending Bank lending to certain central European countries because they have reached an advanced stage of transition towards market economy," she said.
Few of the eastern European speakers directly addressed the question of corruption and inefficiency.

But the representative of the former Soviet republic of Uzbekistan, Rustam Azimov, said the price the ordinary people of central and eastern Europe had to pay for economic reform should not be forgotten.

"The bank could to a fuller extent consider the social costs posed by the implementation of market reforms," he told the meeting. "The price the population is ready to pay for reforms should not exceed the critical point."
